message: Campaign brief: SavvyCal gives a founder explicit control over how soon and how often meetings can be booked through a scheduling link.
reader:
Selected audience: A bootstrapped software founder who sends his own calendar link to clients, partners and investors and winces slightly every time he pastes it.
Research context describes some members of this market, not this recipient's installed tools or experiences. Follow the campaign request when it scopes the job.
Observed situation (grounded; check applicability): Some solo or very small software-company operators personally handle scheduling for sales calls, investor outreach, and casual meeting requests through a single public booking link, without a dedicated scheduling or sales-ops function screening incoming requests.
Qualified campaign scope within that audience: bootstrapped B2B SaaS.
reader_segment: A bootstrapped software founder who sends his own calendar link to clients, partners and investors and winces slightly every time he pastes it
promise: SavvyCal gives a founder explicit control over how soon and how often meetings can be booked through a scheduling link.
arc: In one email, move from the limits of leaving nominally free time open to link bookings, to SavvyCal's minimum-notice and booking-frequency rules, to a focused invitation to test whether those controls fit the founder's calendar boundaries.

emails.job: Earn a SavvyCal account creation so the founder can evaluate whether its minimum-notice and booking-frequency rules match the boundaries needed around link-booked meetings.
emails.single_idea: SavvyCal is worth evaluating because a founder can require advance notice and cap how many meetings a scheduling link accepts per day, week, or month.
emails.selection_reason: Minimum-notice and booking-frequency rules give a founder a concrete, campaign-safe reason to evaluate SavvyCal: they govern how soon and how often an open link may place meetings on the calendar without assuming a named incumbent or a past scheduling disaster.
emails.argument_issue: These rules govern timing and booking volume for anyone using the link. The evidence does not establish automatic prioritization based on the booker's identity, relationship, or importance.
must_not_say: SavvyCal automatically gives clients, prospects, partners, or investors better slots than lower-priority contacts.
SavvyCal identifies, ranks, or screens bookers by importance.
SavvyCal prevents every interruption, calendar collision, or fragmented workday.
The recipient currently experiences seven meetings per day or has had a booking land 30 minutes before a critical meeting.
The reader uses Calendly or any other named incumbent.
Frequency limits distinguish among people using the same link.
These controls improve revenue, meeting quality, productivity, or conversion rates.
Pricing, free-tier access, or no-credit-card terms not included in the campaign-safe claim boundary.
Calendar Overlay, custom domains, branding controls, integrations, workflows, polls, or other unrelated features.

These mechanisms govern when and how often anyone may book and allow separate links per relationship; prioritising slots by who the booker is is not established by the selected evidence, so the 'some people matter more' half of the problem stays unaddressed.

emails.felt_need: A single public booking link treats every incoming request as equal priority, letting an unfamiliar or low-priority booker land a slot that collides with or displaces a high-stakes meeting.
emails.mechanism: SavvyCal's Minimum Notice setting requires a chosen amount of lead time before a new event. Its scheduling-frequency control can impose one or more caps on events booked through a link per day, week, or month. These are explicit timing and volume rules, not identity-based prioritization.
emails.next_step_decision: Decide whether SavvyCal's minimum-notice and booking-frequency rules match the boundaries the founder wants around link-booked meetings.
emails.next_step_value: Creating an account begins a hands-on evaluation of requiring lead time before meetings and capping bookings through a link by day, week, or month.
emails.next_step_limit: The evaluation does not establish automatic prioritization by the booker's identity or relationship to the founder.

alternative_arguments.selection_reason: Proposed-time snippets offer a distinct, documented evaluation proposition for founders who dislike leading with a bare scheduling link: they can present concrete times in the message while retaining a short selection flow.
alternative_arguments.argument_issue: The evidence establishes the proposed-time workflow, but not that cold or high-trust recipients experience it as more personal or collaborative.
alternative_arguments.single_idea: Evaluate SavvyCal as a way to propose specific meeting times in the message instead of making a bare scheduling link carry the entire interaction.
alternative_arguments.felt_need: Sending a scheduling link instead of personally proposing times feels transactional and impersonal, and this is described as especially awkward in cold outreach and with high-trust clients.
alternative_arguments.mechanism: SavvyCal can generate a text snippet that proposes times; the recipient can then choose a meeting time in two clicks.
alternative_arguments.belief_shift: Before: evaluating another scheduling tool only means evaluating another bare booking link. After: SavvyCal also provides a concrete proposed-time flow worth testing in the founder's outreach.
must_not_say: Recipients will consider the proposed-time snippet more personal, polite, collaborative, or appropriate for high-trust conversations.
The workflow eliminates the social awkwardness of scheduling links.
Every recipient prefers proposed times.
The reader currently uses Calendly or another named scheduling product.
The snippet improves response, booking, or conversion rates.

message: Email 1, draft 1: "Control when your link books"
subject: Control when your link books
preview_text: Set minimum notice and cap bookings by day, week, or month.
body:
Set how soon and how often someone can book through your link with SavvyCal. It’s online meeting scheduling software that lets you put explicit boundaries around client, partner, or investor calls.

Choose a minimum-notice window so a new meeting needs the lead time you set. Then switch on scheduling-frequency limits to cap link-booked events by day, week, or month—and combine more than one cap if that suits your calendar.

Create an account to try those controls on a scheduling link. You’ll see whether the lead-time and booking-volume rules match the boundaries you want around your week.

message: Email 1, draft 1: "Propose times in the message"
subject: Propose times in the message
preview_text: Let prospects choose from concrete options in two clicks.
body:
SavvyCal can generate a text snippet with proposed meeting times in seconds. Paste those concrete options into your message, and a prospect can choose a time in two clicks.

It’s online meeting scheduling software, but the invitation doesn’t have to begin with a bare booking link. You propose the times in the message; they follow the short selection flow.

Creating an account lets you test that flow yourself: generate one proposed-time snippet, then decide whether it fits how you invite clients, partners, or investors to meet.

That gives you a concrete alternative to evaluate alongside a standard scheduling link.

issues.detail: the email asks the reader to 'Create a SavvyCal account', which is not one of the actions this product supports (Try SavvyCal risk-free, Sign up, Join SavvyCal, See plans & pricing, Check out the documentation, Read more, Contact Us)

message: Email 1: critic says revise - Do not send this account-creation pitch until the campaign can show the proposed-time artifact and recipient flow it asks readers to sign up to evaluate.
strategy_gap: The fixed /signup step asks cold readers to create an account before they can inspect the proposition’s central object: an actual proposed-time snippet and the recipient’s two-click experience. No supplied sample, preview resource, or supported preview destination closes that gap.
critique_summary: Do not send this account-creation pitch until the campaign can show the proposed-time artifact and recipient flow it asks readers to sign up to evaluate.

edits.line: That gives you a concrete alternative to evaluate alongside a standard scheduling link.
edits.problem: This repeats the proposition after the account request without adding evidence or reducing the evaluation friction that stopped the readers.
edits.fix: Remove the sentence; it contributes nothing needed to reach the ask.

message: Campaign brief: SavvyCal is worth evaluating when a founder wants a free, ad-free meeting poll for the simple job of letting people vote on suitable times.
reader:
Selected audience: A bootstrapped software founder who sends his own calendar link to clients, partners and investors and winces slightly every time he pastes it.
Research context describes some members of this market, not this recipient's installed tools or experiences. Follow the campaign request when it scopes the job.
Observed situation (grounded; check applicability): Some solo or very small software-company operators personally handle scheduling for sales calls, investor outreach, and casual meeting requests through a single public booking link, without a dedicated scheduling or sales-ops function screening incoming requests.
Qualified campaign scope within that audience: bootstrapped B2B SaaS.
reader_segment: A bootstrapped software founder who sends his own calendar link to clients, partners and investors and winces slightly every time he pastes it
promise: SavvyCal is worth evaluating when a founder wants a free, ad-free meeting poll for the simple job of letting people vote on suitable times.
arc: Move the reader from seeing scheduling software as unnecessarily elaborate for agreeing on one time to recognizing one narrow SavvyCal use case they can evaluate: invite people to vote on suitable times with a free, ad-free meeting poll.

emails.job: Earn account creation for a bounded evaluation of SavvyCal's free meeting polls.
emails.single_idea: When the job is simply to settle on a time, SavvyCal offers free, ad-free meeting polls that let people vote on the times that work for them.
emails.selection_reason: The audience research identifies occasions when scheduling software feels excessive for simply agreeing on one time. SavvyCal's documented free, ad-free meeting polls give this self-directed founder a specific and bounded reason to create an account and evaluate the product.
emails.argument_issue: The destination requires account creation, and no supplied evidence establishes a pre-signup poll preview, the effort required to configure a poll, or how recipients will perceive the experience.
emails.objection: Do I need to pay for a full scheduling setup just to coordinate one meeting? Answer narrowly: SavvyCal documents its meeting polls as free and ad-free, while signup and any configuration effort remain part of the evaluation.
must_not_say: Do not claim meeting polls eliminate scheduling back-and-forth, guarantee agreement, save a measured amount of time, or require no configuration.
Do not claim recipients find meeting polls more personal, collaborative, polite, or less status-asserting than scheduling links.
Do not state or imply that this recipient currently uses Calendly or any other named scheduling product.
Do not claim the reader has abandoned a booking link, experienced seven meetings in a day, or had a booking disrupt an important meeting.
Do not promise a pre-signup poll preview or an inspectable recipient experience before account creation.
Do not claim account creation is unnecessary, instant, or requires no credit card.
Do not generalize the free offer beyond SavvyCal meeting polls or imply that every SavvyCal feature is free.

Do not introduce Calendar Overlay, proposed-time snippets, buffers, frequency limits, custom domains, branding, workflows, integrations, paid bookings, pricing, customer counts, or competitor comparisons.
Do not promise effortless migration, automatic transfer of existing links, or compatibility with the reader's current tools.

Free, ad-free meeting polls address only the simple polling use case; they do not establish a lightweight flow elsewhere in the product or resolve the broader social objections to sending scheduling links.

Proposed-time snippets and meeting polls are documented alternatives to pasting a link, but it remains a scheduling tool and no selected evidence shows cold-outreach or high-trust recipients experience it as collaborative.

Free ad-free polls, reminders/workflows and unlimited links on Basic cover part of the complaint, but custom domains and paid bookings are Premium-only additions, the selected evidence gives no plan prices (only 'save 2 months' annually), and no lightweight flow outside meeting polls avoids configuring a link.
emails.felt_need: Scheduling tools are experienced as overkill for the simple case of agreeing on one time, with useful features gated behind extra cost or extra tools.
emails.mechanism: SavvyCal meeting polls present candidate times and invite people to vote on the options that work best for them. The supported evaluation is limited to whether this free, ad-free format suits the founder's occasional group-coordination needs.
emails.next_step_decision: Decide whether SavvyCal's free meeting-poll format is useful for occasions when several people need to settle on a time.
emails.next_step_value: After creating an account, the reader can evaluate a documented meeting-poll capability that invites people to vote on suitable times and is available free without ads.
emails.next_step_limit: The /signup step requires account creation and offers no verified pre-signup poll preview. It does not establish setup effort, recipient sentiment, agreement rates, suitability for the founder's full scheduling workflow, or the terms of other SavvyCal features.

message: Email 1, draft 1: "A free poll for meeting times"
subject: A free poll for meeting times
preview_text: Let clients, partners, or investors vote on suitable options.
body:
When several people need to settle on a time, use a free SavvyCal meeting poll. Add candidate times, then invite everyone to vote on the options that work best for them.

SavvyCal is online meeting scheduling software, but you don’t need to evaluate a full scheduling setup for this particular job. Its meeting polls are **free and ad-free**.

After creating an account, you can try the poll format for one conversation involving several people. That gives you a bounded way to decide whether collecting votes suits the occasional client, partner, or investor meeting that needs a shared time—without turning this into a decision about your entire booking workflow.
